doc.title: Clyde Kerr Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 22, 2006

title: Breaking the rules, trusting the ear, and teaching students to think
summary: If it sounds right it is right; Debussy and Ravel broke rules; education should teach thinking; live performance gives no do-overs.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: What happens when a student comes to you and — this has happened to me — they ask me about something that I don’t use and that I actually don’t know that much about. It could be modes or it could be certain kinds of — they ask me, “When do I use an
enharmonic scale” or something. And I don’t use them, so I’m sometimes stumped as to what to say to that person.

Well I always tell them to look at the notes that are involved. I mean the notes themselves will give you the answers. And when it comes down initially to how does it sound, because the ear is the final judge of that. And you may go by the rules all the time but I mean a lot of rules have been broken because this sounds a certain way and if it sounds right then it’s right. And if that’s the way you want to go nobody can dispute that from you, you say well that’s what I meant to do, that’s the way I wanted to go. You say okay, that’s it. It’s yours. I try to give them many different ways to approach things but I always say look at the notes that are involved and hear the sound. If it sounds right then it’s right. That’s it. Because you could get caught up in the rules and regulations so much, and if we did that all the time we would have never had a Louis Armstrong, Charlie Parker and all because they went beyond the rules. I mean Debussy and Ravel and all those guys, they broke the rules of the guys before them and they weren’t popular at their particular time because they were using whole tone scales and all the sounds that they were using. And thank God for that. Otherwise everybody would sound the same. You’ve got to follow your own instincts in other words. Because I really believe education, no matter if you’re teaching music, you’re teaching science or math, you’re trying to teach a person to think and make judgements for themselves. You know once you’ve done that then you’ve done your job. I want to give you enough information so when you get out on your own you can make the most logical judgement and decision for yourself, and that’s what it’s all about. I said this today with the kids. I could show you or give you cliches and all that but like the thing is you can feed a man, but if you teach him how to fish then he can feed himself. So we’re trying to teach these youngsters how to think. And to me the overall thing in this country is they don’t want education to work because they don’t want people to think for themselves. Because once you start thinking you can see all the bull that they’re trying to pull on you, you know. You may have a Ph.D. but if you can’t really think and see, I mean you can go for anything man. So I don’t think, especially with the arts, if you’re dealing with the arts and you’re really dealing with the arts and you’re looking for the truth, you’re always looking for the truth, then you’re going to see everything. So if we keep people from becoming artists and being able to think and develop their own expression then you can control them in some kind of way. Just because it’s in the paper or you see it on T.V. doesn’t make it right. You have to see that and try to figure it out for yourself. So I think education in general is to teach a person to think and make the correct decisions for themselves. And especially with jazz being in the moment, and it’s going by like that, you have to think quick and you have all these possibilities that can go in that particular moment but this is what I choose at this

particular time. And once it’s out you say well there it is. And if you record it there it is. We can’t — “well let’s do it again.” You can do that in the recording studio but if you’re playing a live performance you can’t. I told a kid that — “wait minute, stop the band, I didn’t mean to play that, start again.” You’re in a night club. You can’t do that.
That’s right. You have to learn how to deal with what you might have thought — I didn’t mean to do that but now I’m going to make it sound like I did.
